title: Logic and fallacies
description: Tell a valid argument from a bad one, and name the usual ways reasoning goes wrong.

ideas.title: Arguments and their parts
ideas.summary: An argument offers premises as reasons for a conclusion; it is sound when it is valid and its premises are true.

items.q: In logic, what makes an argument valid?
items.a: If its premises are true, its conclusion must be true

items.q: In logic, what makes an argument sound?
items.a: It is valid and all its premises are true

items.q: What is the difference between deductive and inductive reasoning?
items.a: Deduction guarantees its conclusion; induction only makes it probable, generalizing from observed cases

items.q: "All fish can fly; a trout is a fish; so a trout can fly." This argument is valid. Why is it not sound?
items.a: Its first premise is false

ideas.title: Valid forms
ideas.summary: A few simple patterns, such as modus ponens and modus tollens, guarantee their conclusions whatever the subject.

items.q: What is the form of the argument called modus ponens?
items.a: If P then Q; P; therefore Q

items.q: What is the form of the argument called modus tollens?
items.a: If P then Q; not Q; therefore not P

items.q: What is the contrapositive of "if P then Q", the statement logically equivalent to it?
items.a: If not Q then not P

items.q: "If it rained, the street is wet. The street is dry. So it did not rain." Which valid form of argument is this?
items.a: Modus tollens

items.q: In the statement "if P then Q", which is the sufficient condition and which the necessary one?
items.a: P is sufficient for Q; Q is necessary for P

ideas.title: Formal fallacies
ideas.summary: Some arguments resemble valid forms but are not: the conclusion does not follow even if every premise is true.

items.q: "If it rained, the street is wet. The street is wet. So it rained." Which formal fallacy is this?
items.a: Affirming the consequent

items.q: "If it rained, the street is wet. It did not rain. So the street is not wet." Which formal fallacy is this?
items.a: Denying the antecedent

items.q: What is the converse of "if P then Q", a statement that does not follow from it?
items.a: If Q then P

items.q: What does the Latin term "non sequitur" mean in logic?
items.a: "It does not follow": a conclusion that does not follow from the premises

ideas.title: Fallacies of relevance
ideas.summary: Many bad arguments attack, flatter or distract instead of addressing the claim itself.

items.q: What is an ad hominem fallacy?
items.a: Attacking the person who makes an argument instead of the argument

items.q: What is a straw man argument?
items.a: Misrepresenting an opponent's position as a weaker one, then attacking that

items.q: Which fallacy argues that a claim is true because many people believe it?
items.a: Appeal to popularity (ad populum, the bandwagon fallacy)

items.q: In an argument, what is a red herring?
items.a: An irrelevant point brought in to distract from the issue

items.q: What is the opposite of a straw man: answering the strongest version of an opponent's view?
items.a: Steelmanning

ideas.title: Fallacies of assumption and evidence
ideas.summary: Other fallacies smuggle in the conclusion, offer too few options, shift a word's meaning, or infer causes too quickly.

items.q: In its strict logical sense, what is begging the question?
items.a: Assuming the conclusion in the premises; circular reasoning

items.q: What is a false dilemma?
items.a: Presenting only two options when more exist

items.q: What does "post hoc ergo propter hoc" mean, and what is the error?
items.a: "After this, therefore because of this": assuming that what came first caused what followed

items.q: What is the slippery slope fallacy?
items.a: Claiming without support that one step will inevitably lead to a chain of extreme results

items.q: Ice cream sales and drownings rise together in summer. What error is it to conclude that ice cream causes drowning?
items.a: Confusing correlation with causation (hot weather causes both)

items.q: What is the fallacy of equivocation?
items.a: Using a word in two different senses within one argument
